items.body: Rebecca Crozier, 27, of Meridian, Idaho, poses in October 2026 with mementos from her baby, Haven. At 11 weeks, she received a fatal fetal diagnosis of anencephaly, and had to travel out of state to terminate the pregnancy because of her state’s near-total abortion ban. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Stateline) MERIDIAN, Idaho — It didn’t take long for doctors to see that something was amiss with Rebecca Crozier’s pregnancy. At her eight-week ultrasound in 2025, they mentioned a possible neural tube defect, she said, but after some research, she thought it was something that could be managed or treated. “If it was a fixable problem, I was ready to quit my job and full-time care for a disabled child,” said Crozier, who is now 27. “That was something that we were prepared to do.” In the time between the two ultrasounds, she had a dream that she was carrying a baby girl, and she and her husband named her Haven. The couple lived in eastern Idaho at the time, and drove two hours to the Boise area to see the maternal-fetal medicine specialists at St. Luke’s, the state’s largest health system. Now at 11 weeks’ gestation, the specialists told her Haven had anencephaly, which occurs when the brain does not develop normally and the skull is left open, exposing brain tissue to amniotic fluid that causes the tissue to dissolve. It is a fatal condition. Rebecca Crozier takes a photo of her belly during her pregnancy before she and her husband, Kris, were told that the fetus would not survive. (Courtesy of Rebecca Crozier) “She was missing a lot of brain tissue,” Crozier recalled. “They were very clear that this baby will not go home with you. You will not take this baby home. This baby will die in the hospital if the baby survives that long.” In many states, even ones with abortion bans, Crozier would have had the option to terminate the pregnancy. But Idaho’s near-total prohibition includes no exceptions for fatal anomalies. It’s one of 11 states that do not have exceptions for anencephaly or other fatal anomalies. Next Tuesday, Idahoans will vote to determine whether the state’s near-total abortion ban should remain the law. Proposition 1, the title of the citizen-led ballot measure, would restore access to abortion until fetal viability, which was the state law before the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022. Idaho is the only state this election cycle with an initiative that would restore access in a state with a ban. In Missouri, voters will consider a different initiative — to reinstate a near-total ban after passing a constitutional amendment in 2024 allowing abortion access until viability. If Idaho’s measure passes, patients like Crozier would no longer have to leave the state for an abortion. According to the Cleveland Clinic, the rate of anencephaly among newborns is about 1 in 10,000, and those babies die within a few hours or days. Most cases end in miscarriage or stillbirth; the fatal birth defect affects about 1 in 1,000 pregnancies. Crozier’s was among them. He wrote that if they had decided to continue the pregnancy, every appointment thereafter could potentially be the one where they discovered Haven had died. “For us, our choice wasn’t whether to let her go or whether she would pass. items.body: (UPDATED, 1 p.m. Wednesday, with corrected information on Idaho’s second-year grant. This grant has not yet been set.) The state of Idaho has awarded $186 million in federal rural healthcare grants — with more than $20 million going into education-related programs. On Wednesday — three days before the feds’ deadline — state officials announced that the first-year grant process was a wrap. “I’m proud of the work that brought us to this point, and I’m excited to see these investments improve care for Idaho families across our state,” said Sen. Julie VanOrden, R-Pingree, the co-chair of a legislative oversight committee that has reviewed the grant applications. Year One: Some highlights The two biggest education-related awards have been in the works for some time . About $12.5 million will go into a suite of 11 initiatives to encourage rural students to pursue healthcare careers. Most of these programs are co-ops involving multiple colleges and universities. The biggest of the group is a $4.3 million Boise State University-led mobile simulation lab project, designed to bring clinical training into rural communities. The State Board of Education will receive $8 million for graduate medical education — rural fellowships and residencies for medical school graduates. Here’s a look at some other education-related grants: The University of Idaho will receive $2 million to create a statewide chronic disease education network. Idaho State University will receive $2 million for a cognitive care pathway network. The U of I and Eat Smart Idaho will share nearly $1.6 million for chronic disease prevention and cancer screening programs. Another U of I grant, of close to $1.2 million, will go toward a pediatric psychiatric assistance line and mental and behavioral health programs. Idaho Educational Services for the Deaf and the Blind will receive nearly $900,000 for a mobile pediatric clinic, which will provide specialized hearing testing in rural Idaho. “For many Idaho families — especially in rural areas — affordable, accessible health care is a real concern,” Gov. Brad Little said in a news release touting the first-year grants. “This investment recognizes those challenges and puts resources where they’re needed most.” Year Two funding: No news yet There was some considerable confusion Wednesday about Idaho’s second-year grant. On Wednesday, as state officials announced the wrapup of their first-year grant program, the Trump administration issued a news release that at least implied an additional $186 million was on its way. “Today, the Trump Administration announced nearly $186 million in Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) funding to improve healthcare access across rural Idaho,” the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services news release said. However, the release simply referred, again, to the first-year grant, which was awarded in December . Idaho won’t find out about its second-year grant for at least a few more weeks. The federal grants are competitive — meaning funding could increase or decrease based on a state’s first-year track record. That’s why Idaho officials and the legislative oversight committee emphasized the importance of meeting the feds’ reporting requirements and hitting the Oct. 30 grant deadline. Idaho potentially has some unfinished business heading into the second year, on at least two education initiatives. The legislative oversight committee discussed the idea of putting some federal money into the undergraduate end of medical education — subsidizing medical school tuition for Idaho students. The idea came up during a July committee meeting , but it never went anywhere. In September, the committee spiked a $1.2 million program with an education nexus. Lawmakers put the brakes on grants that would cover in-school behavioral health hubs — to the chagrin of some of the 10 school districts and charters that applied for a piece of the funding. items.body: Voters cast their ballots in the May 19, 2026, primary election at Emerson High School in Idaho Falls. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) How competitive is the race to represent Idaho in the U.S. Senate? It depends which poll you look at. According to a poll released last week by the campaign for Todd Achilles, an independent running for U.S. Senate, Republican incumbent Jim Risch has only a six-point lead over Achilles. Eight percent of voters were undecided, the poll found. The poll buoyed a claim by the Achilles campaign: Victory could be within reach. State Rep. Todd Achilles speaks from the House floor on the morning of March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “That tight margin confirms what we’re hearing in every corner of Idaho: voters are tired of career politicians controlled by their party bosses,” Achilles, 58, said in a statement with the poll’s release on Oct. 23. But the latest poll didn’t ask about support for the other two candidates in the race, which has drawn one of the most active attempts in years at unseating Risch, 83, who’s seeking a fourth, six-year-term. And Risch’s campaign polling — featuring the full line up of candidates — shows him pummeling Achilles. In the run up to Election Day in a state without much independent polling, that’s the sort of divide in polling outcomes that some pollsters expect voters to see. “Usually about this time, the candidates or the campaigns for ballot issues are publishing polls that show you that they’re going to win,” Stuart Elway, a longtime independent pollster in Washington state, said in an interview. In Idaho, independent political polls — which aren’t backed by a campaign or a special interest group — are hard to come by. They would offer a different perspective, Elway said. Stuart Elway, a retired longtime independent pollster in Washington state, speaks to journalists ahead of the 2023 legislative session in Washington. (Photo courtesy of Stuart Elway) “An independent poll that’s not sponsored by any party or candidate or interest group gives you an objective measure of how the election is going, and I think more importantly, what the people are thinking about when they’re thinking about the election,” he said. Some polling experts say that Idaho lacks independent polls because the state is reliably Republican controlled, and independent pollsters aren’t willing to invest the high funds needed to conduct reliable polling. Instead, there are candidate and special interest groups polling in Idaho, like the back and forth of polls released by the campaigns of Risch and Achilles. The poll released last week by Achilles’ campaign, conducted by VoteNexus , had info on other races — including 54% opposition for Proposition 1, a ballot initiative to end Idaho’s strict abortion ban. In other key races, like for governor, and two U.S. House seats, Republicans were in the lead. The survey, conducted via online polls sent by text message of 700 likely Idaho voters, had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.5 percentage points. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. That’s because certain wording or prefaces can push people toward certain answers. items.body: An influenza vaccine is pictured at the Ellis R. Shipp Public Health Center in West Valley City on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) Idaho health officials on Tuesday reported the state’s second flu death in the 2026-27 influenza season. The death was of a resident of Elmore County, a rural area outside Boise, who was in their 80s, the regional health agency, Central District Health, announced. The first death, reported last week, was of an Owyhee County man who was older than age 65. The deaths come as public health officials say that influenza is spreading earlier in the year than usual. In recent weeks, emergency department and urgent care visits related to the flu have been higher than they were during the same time last year, state health officials say. Idaho has averaged about 60 reported influenza-related deaths annually for the last five flu seasons, with most reported deaths among people over 50, according to the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare. Officials at Central District Health say vaccination is the best way to reduce the risk of severe flu illness. “While most people who get the flu recover without serious complications, some groups are at higher risk for severe illness, hospitalization, and death,” said Dr. Jaime Butler-Dawson, the health district’s epidemiology program manager. “These include adults age 65 and older, pregnant people, young children, people with obesity, and those with weakened immune systems or chronic conditions such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), diabetes, or kidney disease.” According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, this year’s vaccines are designed to protect against three different influenza viruses expected to circulate during the flu season. Symptoms of the flu include fever, cough, sore throat, runny nose, body aches, headache, chills and fatigue. Although most people who get the flu recover after a few days, some can have serious complications that can lead to hospitalization or death. items.body: The College of Western Idaho says its first major fundraising campaign was a $33 million success. On Tuesday, CWI said its Powering the Treasure Valley campaign had exceeded its $30 million goal — funding capital projects and scholarships at the state’s largest community college. “This campaign has always been about our students,” CWI President Gordon Jones said in a news release Tuesday. “Every gift has helped create more opportunities for students to pursue an education, develop the skills employers need, and build a future close to home.” The campaign, launched in July 2023, will leave an imprint across CWI’s landscape. Money will go toward three capital projects on the Nampa campus: The campaign helped fund the Norco Health & Science Building and Agricultural Sciences Complex , which both opened in 2025, and the CapEd Student Success Center, a student services complex that opened earlier this year. Campaign funds will also go toward the CWI downtown Boise campus and the Micron Academic Center , which is expected to open in fall 2027. CWI says the campaign also supports student aid. Since the launch in 2023, CWI has increased its annual scholarship awards from $609,000 to more than $1 million this year. However, the completed fundraising campaign won’t support two other high-profile initiatives on CWI’s radar. This money will not go toward deferred maintenance on the recently acquired Ford Idaho Center , although college officials have said fundraising will be a component in covering the $25 million in maintenance costs. This money also will not go toward an endowment-based initiative to launch CWI’s first intercollegiate athletics programs. “When CWI launched Powering the Treasure Valley … we committed to two priorities: improving the student experience and adding capacity so we can serve more students,” college spokesman Ashley Smith said in a text Tuesday.

items.body: McMillan Elementary can serve 475 students, but just 171 students attend the school today. Enrollment has fallen by 62% since 2014. Class sizes are much smaller than the average across the West Ada School District. Some grade levels only have one class. Taxpayers are subsidizing the cost of heating and cooling empty rooms. The building needs $5.4 million in repairs and updates within 10 years. These are some of the facts that school district staff presented at a school board meeting Monday night to a crowd of parents and community members who are fighting to keep the school open. The school board will make a decision in November to decommission the school or keep it open. David Reinhart, the district’s chief operating officer, said the district built several schools close together on the eastern portion of the district back in the ’70s and ’80s when the population was surging. Schools like McMillan were full for many years. But now the school is 36% full and is projected to continue to decline to 121 students in 2031. “The situation we find ourselves in this eastern portion of our district is that something has to shift no matter what when we have a shrinking population and so many schools in one particular corner,” Reinhart said. “This is really at the heart of the matter.” Nineteen parents, students and community members spoke during the public input portion of the meeting. All opposed closing the school. Paige Wilson, a mother of three McMillan students, started a petition on Change.org to keep the school open. It has 609 signatures. She told trustees on Monday that her daughter struggled at an overcrowded district but has since caught up at McMillan. “We all know McMillan Elementary cares about their students,” Wilson said. “The question is, does the West West Ada School District care about the students?” Paige Wilson, a mother of three students at McMillan Elementary, pleads with the West Ada school board to keep the school open at a meeting on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026, in Meridian. items.title: ‘We don’t have data’: Kuna to evaluate student screen time
items.summary: KUNA – The Kuna School District plans to recommend new guidance on student screen time before the end of the school year as leaders work to determine how much time students spend on computers and other devices, and what they’re doing on those devices. items.body: KUNA – The Kuna School District plans to recommend new guidance on student screen time before the end of the school year as leaders work to determine how much time students spend on computers and other devices, and what they’re doing on those devices. The effort stems from community concerns about too much student screen time, said Kuna Teaching and Learning Director Kevin Gifford. The nearby West Ada district launched a similar initiative in August. “The endgame ultimately is to have a district guidance document with clear goals for what we believe an appropriate balance of screen time would be,” Gifford said. In the meantime, the district has provided some immediate guidance for teachers. Kuna’s teacher guidance A guidance document Gifford distributed to district administrators and teachers provides three “best practices” to implement immediately: Ensure screen time is teacher-planned and directed to reduce “passive consumption.” Provide students with tech-free options during downtime. Collect data on how and when students use digital learning tools and applications. The district hasn’t collected data that clearly show how much time students spend on screens, Gifford told Idaho Education News. Still, national news coverage of instructional software i-Ready led to complaints in Kuna earlier this year, Gifford said. The new initiative to gather data and recommend new rules is, in part, to quell those concerns. Student screen time expanded during the COVID pandemic, when the district largely moved to online learning, putting students on Chromebooks at home. Six years later, district leaders wonder if they are properly balancing screen time with other activities in school. The district will begin measuring student device usage to create a live data report showing districtwide screen time averages. Gifford said the goal is to gather accurate and complete data to “tell the whole story, so that we’re not just reacting to perceptions.” Parts of the initiative start in the coming weeks. The district will guide teachers to ensure students have tech-free options during free time after completing assignments, during recess or between classes. Parents will receive a district survey asking for their opinions on device usage, but the district hasn’t determined when that will happen. Gifford feels the district is also getting ahead of the Legislature, where devices in schools have been a topic of discussion in recent years. In 2025, legislators unanimously approved a law directing school districts to limit students’ access to cellphones. In the 2026 session, lawmakers discussed artificial intelligence in schools but not screen time. Senate Bill 1227 directed the Idaho Department of Education to develop a framework for “responsible use” of AI in K-12 schools. Meanwhile, some educators are evaluating whether certain students should be on computers at all. Idaho Education Technology Association communications coordinator Will Goodman told EdNews in August that the organization plans to lobby for a ban on screens in kindergarten through third grade classrooms. “I know our Legislature is going to be looking at this very topic this year,” Gifford told Kuna trustees at the district’s October board meeting. “It’ll be good for us to be already working toward it.”

items.body: Blaine Conzatti is the president of the Idaho Family Policy Center. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Family Policy Center) Opponents of the proposed abortion rights initiative Proposition 1 filed a lawsuit Monday seeking to pull TV ads paid for by the Idaho Democratic Party in favor of the initiative. The conservative, Christian advocacy organization, the Idaho Family Policy Center, and leaders with a political action committee that opposes the initiative, Too Extreme for Idaho PAC, brought the lawsuit. The ballot initiative Prop 1 would repeal Idaho’s abortion ban, allowing the procedure up to viability or after in cases of emergency, enumerate rights related to a range of reproductive healthcare, and provide legal liability protections for healthcare providers who provide that type of care. The initiative will be before Idaho voters in the Nov. 3 general election. The lawsuit, filed in Canyon County court, alleges that the supporters and authors of Prop 1, a group called Idahoans United for Women and Families, paid the Idaho Democratic Party to run ads in favor of the initiative in order to pay the more favorable rates that broadcasters are required to charge to political candidates ahead of elections. The ads were run on behalf of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Terri Pickens. “Pro-abortion activists cheated their way into cheaper television advertisements to stump for their radical abortion ballot initiative,” Idaho Family Policy Center President Blaine Conzatti said in a written statement. “Instead of playing by the rules of the game as outlined in our state campaign finance laws, Idahoans United for Women and Families colluded with the Idaho Democratic Party to mislead voters and gain an unfair advantage. Idaho voters deserve transparency — not shell games and dirty tricks.” Idaho Democratic Party spokesperson Avery Roberts called the lawsuit “frivolous” in an email to the Idaho Capital Sun. She said it was “another attempt by opponents of Prop 1 to distract from the devastating consequences of Idaho’s extreme abortion ban.” “Women are being forced to leave the state for lifesaving medical care, and the politicians responsible have done nothing to fix it,” Roberts said. “Instead of addressing the harm this ban has caused, opponents are trying to silence the families speaking out, even after the Secretary of State’s Office confirmed our advertising complies with Idaho campaign finance laws. We won’t be intimidated into silence. Idahoans deserve to hear these families’ stories and make up their own minds on November 3.” The family policy center helped author Idaho’s law allowing family members of an aborted fetus to sue the abortion provider for a minimum of $20,000. It has also been a supporter of Idaho’s criminal abortion ban, which includes felony prison penalties for abortion providers. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) The Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane’s office, which oversees statewide elections, told Boise State Public Radio Friday that the ads did not violate campaign finance laws. Secretary of State’s Office spokesperson Joe Parris told the Sun Monday that the office was not investigating an ad about Prop 1 paid for by the Idaho Democrats because it had not received a complaint about it. The lawsuit includes a complaint to the office about financial reporting related to ads paid for by the Pickens campaign, but does not mention Prop 1 or a contribution from Idahoans United. “Our office has not received a complaint on the ad that is at the center of this lawsuit,” Parris said. The Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act would restore abortion access “without government interference” until fetal viability, and would protect fertility treatments and other reproductive care such as contraception. (Photo by Kelcie Moseley-Morris/Stateline) Chrissy Teigen will be in Boise on Wednesday to campaign in favor of Proposition 1 , which would repeal Idaho’s strict abortion ban laws and provide protections for the procedure. Proposition 1, also called the Reproductive Freedom and Privacy Act , also provides protections for access to birth control, in vitro fertilization and privacy in healthcare decisions. Chrissy Teigen (Photo courtesy of Chrissy Teigen) Teigen, who is a New York Times #1 bestselling cookbook author, model, entrepreneur and advocate for maternal health, will meet privately with Idaho mothers to talk with them about how the state’s abortion ban laws have affected them. She’ll then speak at a “Yes on Prop 1” rally, to be held from noon to 1 p.m. Wednesday at Treefort Music Hall, to encourage Idahoans to cast their ballots during the final days of early voting. The Treefort Music Hall is located at 722 W. Broad St. in Downtown Boise, and the rally is open to the public. Idahoans will decide the outcome of Proposition 1 during the Nov. 3 general election. It would take a simple majority of “yes” votes across the state to approve Prop 1. Under Idaho’s abortion ban laws, it is a felony to perform nearly any abortion, except to prevent the death of the mother, or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors in Idaho can be sued for a minimum of $20,000 and be criminally prosecuted for performing an abortion. “In September 2020, Teigen underwent a medically necessary abortion at 20 weeks after experiencing a partial placental abruption, a serious pregnancy complication that put her health at risk,” a press release announcing Teigen’s appearance said. “The pregnancy was deeply wanted, but the baby was not expected to survive, and continuing the pregnancy posed serious risks to Teigen’s health.” Idaho’s abortion ban laws do not carve out an exception to protect a mother’s health, and instead only has an exception to prevent her death. items.body: A former teacher has sued the Boise School District, saying she was made the “fall guy” over a series of sexual abuse complaints. Marianne Baker is seeking at least $10,000 from the district. She says district officials forced her to resign from her special education job at Valley View Elementary School after she reported concerns about Gavin Snow, a paraprofessional who worked for Baker at Valley View. The district has agreed to $7 million in civil settlements to Boise parents who accused Snow of sexual abuse. “(Baker) was made the ‘fall guy’ for the district’s shortcomings and negligent hiring of Gavin Snow,” according to the Oct. 1 lawsuit. “Marianne was stripped of her professional passion and has suffered immense reputational damage that will follow her for the rest of her life.” District spokesman Dan Hollar declined to comment on the lawsuit Monday, because the case is “the subject of ongoing litigation.” The lawsuit presents a timeline of Baker’s final months with the Boise district: December 2024: On three occasions, Baker observes Snow had his phone in the bathroom while helping special education students — in violation of Baker’s policy for paraprofessionals. “Marianne assumed Gavin was being insubordinate by texting during working hours,” the lawsuit says. Jan. 6-7, 2025: Noting a change in Snow’s demeanor, Baker seeks to file a report with then-Valley View Principal Rick Jordan and other officials. Jan. 7, 2025: School counselor Paula Perry announces a new no-phones-in-bathrooms policy. After the meeting, Snow follows Baker into an empty staff room. Fearing for her safety, Baker leaves the room. “It was at that point that Marianne knew Gavin had done something nefarious and/or illegal with the children of her class,” the lawsuit says. Jan. 10, 2025: Jordan and a top district official tell Baker she had done the right thing by reporting Snow, the lawsuit says, “because the detectives had found child pornography on Gavin’s phone and computer at home.” About an hour after this conversation, Baker learns that Snow had taken his own life as Boise police tried to arrest him on child sexual abuse charges. Feb. 21, 2025: The district tells Baker that she is being placed on administrative leave for failing to report child abuse, abandonment or neglect. May 8, 2025: Boise Education Association leaders Lara Luthy and Stephanie Myers tell Baker that the district would be terminating her, giving her the option to resign and receive pay and benefits through September. “Lara and Stephanie informed Marianne that if she resigned, her employment file would be ‘cleaner’ and she would be able to seek employment in a school district elsewhere,” the lawsuit says. May 13, 2025: Baker “reluctantly” signs a letter of resignation. May 20, 2025: Boise district attorney Dan Skinner files a complaint against Baker with the Professional Standards Commission, a volunteer board that can revoke or suspend teaching certificates. June 16, 2025: Baker receives a criminal summons. She is charged with two misdemeanor counts of failing to report suspected abuse. Jan. 5: Magistrate Judge David Manweiler dismisses the misdemeanor counts . That same day, district officials uploaded the PSC complaint to her employment file. In her lawsuit, Baker says she has suffered high blood pressure and anxiety and “significant depression” due to the administrative leave and resignation. She says she now works as a flight attendant and a bartender on weekends, making “significantly less” than what she earned as a teacher. Baker filed a $1 million tort claim in November , as a precursor to the lawsuit.

items.body: An Ada County judge will privately review data spreadsheets compiled by Boise State University researchers before ruling on whether the university must hand them over to an anti-abortion lobbying group. The Idaho Family Policy Center (IFPC) — a Christian lobbying group that helped write Idaho’s restrictive abortion laws — sued Boise State , alleging that it withheld public records related to a widely cited article co-authored by two researchers affiliated with the university. The article said that obstetrician-gynecologists fled Idaho after the state’s abortion ban took effect in 2022. Ada County District Court Judge Nancy Baskin " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/images.jpeg" class="size-full wp-image-127657" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/images.jpeg" alt="" width="150" height="200" /> Ada County District Court Judge Nancy Baskin In December, IFPC filed a records request seeking “all documents” and “all data” related to the article, but Boise State only provided a single, two-page spreadsheet. In a July petition to Ada County’s district court, IFPC argued that the research “must have produced a paper trail longer than two pages.” IFPC’s petition asked the court to compel the university to hand over additional records, including emails along with documents from Boise State’s Institutional Review Board (IRB), which approved the researchers’ process for collecting data on human subjects. District Judge Nancy Baskin heard arguments in the case Friday. Carsten Peterson, an attorney at Hawley Troxell, represented Boise State. While Peterson acknowledged that additional records related to the article exist, including various other data sets, he argued that the university reviewed IFPC’s request “in good faith” and provided the only record that matched its request. After asking the attorneys questions for more than an hour, Baskin ordered Boise State to show her any data files that the university deemed outside the scope of IFPC’s request. Baskin will review the spreadsheets “in-camera,” meaning behind closed doors, before she issues a written ruling on IFPC’s petition. Boise State has 10 days to deliver the spreadsheets to Baskin. Article heavily cited in debate over abortion laws The article, published last year by the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA), reported that 35% of OB-GYNs left Idaho between 2022 and 2024 — after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade, triggering Idaho’s abortion ban. Carsten Peterson, an attorney at Hawley Troxell, a private law firm representing Boise State. (Photo credit: Hawley Troxell) Two researchers affiliated with Boise State — J. Edward McEachern, an adjunct faculty member and doctor at St. Luke’s, and Allen Traylor, a graduate student — co-authored the article with a doctor unaffiliated with the university. They conducted three “ cross-sectional censuses” of OB-GYN physicians practicing obstetrics in Idaho to determine how many left the state after the U.S. Supreme Court decision. The article has been frequently cited in coverage detailing the effects of Idaho’s abortion ban, including by the New York Times last week, and by supporters of Proposition 1.

(Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho lawmakers will weigh whether to fund several drug-prevention and treatment projects, totaling over $3 million, through the state’s endowment fund from tobacco lawsuit settlement money. The legislative Joint Millennium Fund Committee, which oversees the endowment, heard 10 proposals Friday for use of the settlement money, which must go toward drug and alcohol prevention. As of Sept. 30, the fund’s balance was nearly $43.5 million — however, some of the previously approved projects hadn’t yet been funded, according to Senior Budget and Policy Analyst Janica Bisharat. The committee is focused particularly on youth prevention and cessation in approving use of the fund for projects. Sen. Van Burtenshaw, R-Terreton, (right) chats with Sen. Jim Woodward, R-Sagle, on the Senate floor on March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “I am laser-focused on prevention,” committee co-Chair Sen. Van Burtenshaw, R-Terreton, said Friday. “I have three deaths in my family already, and two or three more that are getting close. I’ve seen abuse. I’ve seen the problem, and as long as I have this position, I’m gonna focus on that. And that’s the focus of our group here is prevention.” The committee did not decide on its recommended projects to fund. The funding would need final approval from legislative budget writers on the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee during the legislative session, which begins in January. Here are the proposed projects lawmakers heard Friday: Recovery Idaho asks for $32,780 to create a certification process for recovery centers The nonprofit Recovery Idaho sought just under $33,000 to create a voluntary accreditation program for recovery centers statewide. Recovery centers provide treatment for drug and alcohol addiction and also often provide additional support for clients in treatment. “The problem right now is that the recovery community centers throughout the state are very well intentioned, but there’s a fair amount of variation and maybe not enough tracking of what exactly happens and what those outcomes are,” Andra Smith Hansen, a Recovery Idaho board member, told the committee members. Recovery centers provide support to adults, but many of those adults are parents, Smith Hansen said, and better outcomes for those adults can lead to better outcomes for their children. The money would be used to work with recovery centers statewide to develop standards, a process for accreditation and standardized metrics to evaluate outcomes. items.body: The Pocatello-Chubbuck School District will stick with a five-day school week and trimester schedule after trustees unanimously rejected proposals to adopt a four-day week and semesters. The vote happened at a board meeting Tuesday and follows months of consideration that fleshed out trustees’ preferences for keeping the district’s schedules intact . Trustees discussed a possible change to how the district uses Fridays, but the board took no action. Two trustees proposed exploring different hybrid models, but neither motion received a second. “We have a consensus that we certainly do want to look at the options,” said Board Chair Raymond Knoff. “It probably is too late for us to do that this year.” The change to a four-day week would have made Pocatello-Chubbuck one of the largest districts in Idaho to adopt the model. The similarly sized Nampa district made the switch two years ago. Pocatello-Chubbuck trustees each had their own concerns with the change. Trustee Megan Furniss cited concerns about a lack of input from the district’s families who qualify for free- and reduced-price lunch. Trustee Bill Osborn simply wanted to stay in line with most school districts in the country. “If it was such a good idea, why haven’t more school districts in the past five decades gone after it?” asked Osborn, echoing his statements at a recent meeting. Finances weren’t part of the five-day week or hybrid discussions. “In my opinion, it shouldn’t be part of the conversation,” said district business manager Jonathan Balls, “just because there’s a lot bigger factors out there than the finances.”

items.body: October is Dyslexia Awareness Month in Idaho, and over the past 10 years, Idaho professionals have prioritized early literacy and dyslexia education statewide. From updated, data-driven instruction for incoming teachers to intervention tutoring for elementary students, Boise State University has been at the forefront of these literacy initiatives. In September, Boise State University awarded its first endowed professorship in education to Clinical Associate Professor Carolyn Cort. Her specialty is early literacy. At BSU, Cort teaches courses in the early language and literacy endorsement, which is similar to a minor, for education majors and teacher candidates. The classes instruct teacher candidates how to properly test literacy comprehension and screen for dyslexia. Panelists at Saturday’s Literacy, Language and Dyslexia Summit at BSU. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The director of Idaho’s largest state agency will step down by the end of the year. Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron told employees in a letter she’d be stepping back to provide more support to her family, Boise State Public Radio first reported. Gov. Brad Little’s communication director, Emily Callihan, told BSPR that Charron’s father faced “significant health challenges.” “This has not been an easy decision,” Charron wrote in the letter to employees. “The past year has brought significant challenges for my family, and I realize that they need more of my time, attention, and support. Family has always been important to me, and right now, being there for mine needs to be my priority.” Charron’s last day has not been finalized, and it’s unclear who will serve as interim director when she leaves. Idaho Gov. Brad Little gives a press conference after delivering his annual State of the State address on Jan. 6, 2025, in the Lincoln Auditorium in the Idaho Capitol. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Little appointed Charron as director in July 2025, and she officially stepped into the post in September last year, after previously serving as the agency’s top Medicaid official since 2021, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. “I want to thank Juliet Charron for her outstanding service as Health and Welfare Director,” Little said in a written statement to the Sun. “Under her leadership, the department made meaningful progress in strengthening child welfare prevention, preparing to distribute nearly $200 million in Rural Health Transformation funding in the coming months as part of nearly $1 billion over five years, and improving compliance, accountability, and program outcomes. I appreciate her commitment to serving Idahoans and look forward to announcing new leadership for the state’s largest agency before the end of the year.” Health and Welfare spokesman AJ McWhorter told the Sun the agency had “a number of vacancies in some key positions for a variety of unrelated reasons, including external opportunities, retirements, and personal and family reasons.” “The Governor’s Office will announce a new director at a later date,” McWhorter said. “DHW is hiring for the other positions, and we encourage qualified people to apply. We will continue to focus on the work and provide quality, efficient, and effective services for the people of Idaho.” Before joining Idaho’s health agency, Charron held leadership positions in the Texas Medicaid program and with the Texas Office of Inspector General. She also worked in government programs and “compliance roles” for a community-based health plan in Arizona, according to her biography . Charron leaves Idaho’s largest agency with the biggest budget The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare runs public assistance programs like Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and the Women and Infant Children program. The health department also provides public health services, regulates long-term care facilities, runs the state’s mental health hospitals, provides child welfare and provides services for people with developmental disabilities. The agency’s total budget is more than $5 billion of mostly federal funds. As head of the agency, Charron oversaw some of the beginning stages of the state’s shift to administering Idaho’s entire Medicaid program through private managed care companies , as directed by the Idaho Legislature’s House Bill 345 . The full transition to managed care oversight of Medicaid is expected to happen by 2030. Charron has also overseen the influx of federal funds from the Rural Health Transformation Grant. items.body: How much growth is too much, and too fast? The State Board of Education grappled with that question last week, and couldn’t wrestle it into submission. The board punted on a three-year plan that guides new growth and new programs at the state’s colleges and universities. In its stead, the board gave the schools a one-year go-ahead, enough to let them keep working on new programs for 2027-28. The three-year plan is on hold until the board’s December meeting. Yes, three-year plans are wonky and boring. Until you think about what’s being planned. If you’re a taxpayer, here’s why you ought to care. The whole idea behind the three-year plan is to grow the higher education portfolio in an orderly way — without wasting tax dollars on redundant programs. If you’re student, or soon to be one, here’s why you ought to care. These plans will help determine what you can study, and where, laying out your options for career credentials or a full-blown degree. And if you’re an employer, here’s why you ought to care. Many of the new additions to the three-year plans focus on the state’s hottest job sectors — such as healthcare and cybersecurity. These are the new programs Idaho employers need: pipelines from the campus to the workplace. So the State Board is debating something that sounds dull, but is actually crucial. Who wants what? Here’s what Idaho’s eight colleges and universities hope to add by 2030, according to three-year plans submitted to the State Board of Education. The eight colleges and universities are looking at creating 277 new programs over the next three years. Nearly half of these new adds, 111 in all, are professional certificates, and 61 are career-technical programs. The remaining 105 are undergraduate or graduate degree programs. items.body: Vallivue School District trustees cured two open meeting violations from a meeting last week, appointed a trustee to fill one vacancy and asked the Canyon County Board of Commissioners to fill a second vacancy, as required by law if a board fails to fill a vacancy after 120 days. Trustees appointed Kellie Horrocks at a special meeting Wednesday. The mother of four young children is the new trustee for Zone 4 and replaces Paul Tierney, who resigned in August . Horrocks joined Wednesday’s meeting by phone. “Truth be told, I don’t know a lot about what goes on on the board,” Horrocks said in her interview. Two other candidates — Idaho Power attorney Brian Bishop and restaurant assistant manager Esther Ma, who is also running for the State Senate as a Constitution Party candidate in District 11 — attended in person. “The types of things that the board does are things I do every day in my work,” Bishop said in his interview. Click to view slideshow. Board Chair Jennifer Cox said she liked that Horrocks has young children, bringing a different perspective to the board, and is willing to learn. “She was off-the-hip honest,” Cox said. After conducting the three interviews, trustees deliberated in open session then voted unanimously to appoint Horrocks, which was noticed on the agenda as an action item. Last week, the board handled a vacancy in Zone 3 differently. Resolving open meeting violations The board last week interviewed two candidates to fill the vacancy in Zone 3, left by trustee Toni Brinegar, who resigned in June . Trustees then deliberated and came to a “consensus” to appoint naturopathic medical doctor Brett Butterfield, but the meeting’s agenda did not include an action item to make the appointment. After that meeting, EdNews emailed district leaders to express concerns regarding possible open meeting violations. “Thank you for your patience and thank you for bringing your concerns to our attention,” Finance Director Dalelyn Allen responded last Thursday. At the Wednesday special meeting, the board acknowledged and cured two open meeting violations. Cox read two statements, citing Idaho statute. items.body: From left to right: Coeur d'Alene attorney Arthur "Art" Macomber, former Idaho Congressman Raúl Labrador and incumbent Idaho Attorney General Lawrence Wasden debate on Idaho Public Television on April 19, 2022. (Photo by Aaron Kunz/Idaho Public Television) During the 2026 election cycle, Idaho voters have had very few opportunities to see Republican incumbents answer questions at live, public events. For years it was the norm for major candidates in statewide and federal races to appear live and debate each other. Journalist Betsy Z. Russell asks a candidate question during an Idaho Public Television debate on May 6, 2016. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger) “It was a tradition in Idaho,” said Betsy Russell, former longtime president of the Idaho Press Club and current president for Idahoans for Openness in Government. “That was how candidates, including incumbents seeking reelection, got out there and put their views and how they contrasted with those of their opponents, in front of all voters all across the state of Idaho.” Idaho Public Television, which for years has broadcast its Idaho Debates series statewide, did not have the staffing to put on the events this year, according to Melissa Davlin, IPTV producer and Idaho Press Club president. “I do think there are some incumbents who would have said yes to debates had that been a possibility,” Davlin said. Davlin also noted that there’s a national trend of candidates from both major parties declining debates. Of the 35 U.S. Senate seats up for election this year, 21 of them had no debate between the major candidates, ABC News reported. Similarly, of the 36 governors up for election, 21 of those races had no debate scheduled between two major-party candidates. “This is not Idaho-specific,” Davlin said. “… and you could say a big part of that is the siloing of social media. People who are running for office often have or feel like they have a direct line to voters.” The League of Women Voters of Idaho this year held forums for U.S. Senate candidates and gubernatorial candidates . The Republican incumbents in both of those races declined to participate. U.S. Sen. Jim Risch’s campaign spokesman previously told the Sun that he declined that forum because the individual who reached out to him to ask about participation had endorsed his opponent. The league’s president Jean Henscheid told the Sun that individual, former state Rep. Julie Yamamoto, had reached out in her own capacity and was not one of the event’s organizers. Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho Gov. Brad Little’s campaign manager Joan Vargas did not directly answer a question about why the governor has not participated in debates this election cycle. “Governor Little has a proven track record of providing Idahoans historic tax relief, promoting a strong economy, cutting red tape, responsibly managing state government. On his watch, Idaho has made record investments in schools, roads, water, and other areas. Those historic accomplishments and facts are non-debatable,” Vargas wrote. “Governor Little has made it a priority to meet with Idaho families, businesses, and members of the press. Idahoans know what Governor Little stands for. They know he will continue to fight for them and make our state the place where our children and grandchildren choose to stay.” Little was the only incumbent statewide elected official to not respond to the Idaho Capital Sun’s 2026 general election candidate survey. items.body: Trained teachers and staff will carry guns in Marsing and Homedale schools after trustees in both districts unanimously approved policies last week. The armed staff policies are modeled after one in the Kimberly School District , which rolled out its program last year. The policies are all identical, word-for-word, except for the districts’ names. “This Policy is only to aid Homedale School District in deterring, detecting, and denying some type of active shooter incident from occurring on school property,” Homedale’s policy reads. Approved staff members carrying a firearm will “be responsible to defend, using deadly force, if necessary, their zone of responsibility.” The Homedale and Marsing school boards must now approve individual staff members to carry a concealed firearm on campus. Criteria for approval include: Possession of a current Idaho Enhanced Concealed Weapon License A recommendation from the superintendent A physical and psychological assessment The board can deny permission for any reason and will review staff members’ grants of permission annually. Once approved, employees must complete at least 40 hours of training. “Training will include engagement on the range with a certified instructor in live fire situations that require ‘shoot, don’t shoot’ decision making and other dynamic scenarios,” the policy says. District leaders said they heard mostly positive feedback from community members. “Every community member that I’ve talked to … has been super positive, saying we should’ve done this years ago,” Marsing Board Chair Jason Sevy told Idaho Education News. On Monday, after approving the policy, Homedale held a community meeting to gather feedback. Dwayne Fisher told EdNews he only heard positive feedback. Trustees in both districts had been considering the policy for years. Marsing surveyed its employees in 2022 but didn’t act until this year. Days after both districts approved their policies, a school shooter killed four people at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon. Megan Lambert , a Boise State University graduate and special education teacher, died in the shooting. “W ith what just happened in Bend, u nfortunately, it’s on the forefront of everyone’s minds again,” Fisher said. “More than anything, we’re hoping that people know our schools are not going to be soft targets.” Both districts have begun installing signs showing that staff members may be armed.

items.body: Officials from Idaho Power, Rocky Mountain Power and Avista told members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission that nuclear energy can provide a reliable and clean source of energy that diversifies energy portfolios, but high costs to build such projects can create barriers. (Photo by Gregory Thomas/USDA) High costs and lengthy permitting processes are two of the barriers to bringing nuclear-powered electricity to customers in Idaho, officials from three electrical utilities told state regulators during a public forum outside of Boise on Tuesday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Officials from Idaho Power, Rocky Mountain Power and Avista told members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission that nuclear energy can provide a reliable and clean source of energy that diversifies energy portfolios. However, the high cost to build nuclear power projects, the absence of price certainty and permitting processes that can stretch for 10 years or longer do not align with state regulators’ “least cost, least risk” mandate. “When I think of the benefits of nuclear, I think diversity is a huge part of it,” Idaho Power Chief Operating Officer Adam Richins said. “Obviously, it’s dispatchable clean energy, which really doesn’t exist besides nuclear.” Adam Richins was named Idaho Power’s executive vice president and chief operating officer in February 2026 after previously serving in other roles at the utility. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Power) “On the other side of the spectrum … right now we don’t know how much it’s going to cost, and obviously when you talk about ‘least cost, least risk,’ that is very important,” Richins said. For example, Richins said the expansion of Plant Vogtle nuclear power plant in Georgia ran over budget by $16 billion to $21 billion. The Idaho Public Utilities Commission sets rates and regulates investor-owned and privately-owned utilities that provide electricity, gas, water or some telephone services for a profit. The three members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission, or PUC for short, are appointed by the governor. None of the three companies use nuclear in their energy mix. But Rocky Mountain Power officials recently announced a 40-year power purchase agreement to buy electricity from a TerraPower nuclear power plant that is being built in Kemmerer, Wyoming. The Wyoming plant is being built at the site of a coal plant that is being retired, with about $2 billion in federal funding from the U.S. Department of Energy supporting the project. The Idaho Public Utilities Commission did not have any specific nuclear energy proposals under consideration during Tuesday’s forum and did not take any action. “The primary purpose of this opportunity for us is to listen to each and every one (of the utilities participating in the forum),” Idaho PUC Chairman Edward Lodge said. items.body: A 46-year-old graduate student, a 12-year-old homeschooler and an 18-year-old college freshman gathered with others on a sunny Tuesday afternoon at Moscow High to kick off the last week of an archeological dig. The dig is part of a continuing push by the university’s anthropology department to help Idahoans connect to their own history through archeology — and connect with each other through a shared interest. This fall marks the third time the group has dug at the high school, built in the 1930s. Organizers say it was also the most productive, with students discovering a corner of the original 1890 school that was demolished years ago to make way for the current high school. Students also dug in what was once an alley behind area homes, uncovering artifacts of daily life, like buttons, a doll face and remnants of dishes. Graduate students recently started a project underneath Moscow’s public library, where they discovered hundreds of intact literary artifacts, like bookbinding supplies, ink pads and lightbulbs. The program provides students with real-world experience that is typically offered through a field school, where they often pay to travel to a remote location to complete a dig during a school break. Other community members are also welcome to participate. “It gives them more than just the skills training — it gives them the why,” said Katrina Eichner, associate professor of anthropology. “It’s not just fun for us to play in the dirt. This is important to people because it’s their history.” University of Idaho anthropology professors Katrina Eichner and Renae Campbell help students at an archaeological dig at Moscow High. McGrane, a seasoned Idaho election official seeking a second term, says he’s running on a track record of keeping elections secure and improving access to election information. The two will be on the ballot in the Nov. 3 general election. The secretary of state is a statewide office that oversees elections in the state, manages campaign finance compliance and transparency, and maintains records on businesses. The secretary of state also serves on the Land Board, which manages the state’s endowment lands. The secretary of state serves a four-year term and earns an annual salary of $128,690. Educational exhibits are placed along the trail to provide information. (Photo courtesy of the National Park Service) The Friends of Minidoka nonprofit will host its 2026 symposium, which will feature a film screening, legal discussion and lecture, “to consider the enduring importance of due process, equal protection, and civic engagement in protecting our civil liberties and strengthening democracy,” according to a press release from the organization. The 2026 Civil Liberties Symposium, titled Law, Civil Liberties, and the Continuing Pursuit of Justice: From Wayne Collins to Today, will examine how “the unjust incarceration of Japanese Americans during World War II continues to inform contemporary debates surrounding immigration, detention, national security, and constitutional rights,” the press release said. In 1942, the Minidoka War Relocation Center was constructed in Jerome County at Hunt, Idaho. Locally, it was known as “Hunt Camp.” While in operation, the site was the seventh largest city in Idaho, incarcerating nearly 9,400 people at its peak population. (Photo courtesy of the National Archives and Records Administration) The series begins Thursday with a screening of “Wayne Collins: One Fighting Irishman,” a 30-minute documentary about the San Francisco attorney who spent more than two decades defending Japanese Americans who renounced their U.S. citizenship under duress while imprisoned at the Tule Lake Segregation Center during World War II. The screening will be followed by a discussion with Emily Croston, staff attorney with the ACLU of Idaho, and Wendy Olson, former U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho and chairwoman of the Idaho State Bar’s Diversity Section. On Nov. 5, the group will host its 2026 distinguished lecture: “Mass Deportation, Detention, and ICE: How We Got Here and What We Can Do,” presented by Kari Hong, the director of the Immigration Law Clinic at the University of Idaho College of Law. Drawing on her experience as an immigration attorney, public interest lawyer, and legal scholar, Hong will examine the history and present-day realities of immigration enforcement and detention, along with opportunities to protect the rights of affected individuals. The lecture will be followed by a moderated Q&A session with the audience. The symposium concludes Dec. 8 with an online presentation of Hong’s distinguished lecture, offering another opportunity for community members to participate and engage with these issues. “History reminds us that civil liberties can be threatened when fear and claims of national security are used to justify the erosion of constitutional protections,” said Robyn Achilles, executive director of Friends of Minidoka. “By bringing historical perspectives into conversation with today’s legal challenges, the Civil Liberties Symposium creates opportunities for our community to learn, ask difficult questions, and consider our shared responsibility to uphold justice.” All events are free and open to the public, with registration required. items.body: An orange "detour ahead" sign alerts motorists of a new route around new housing construction in Boise in summer 2026. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s newly approved Opportunity Zones could help bring more housing, businesses and jobs to communities across the state. The attraction for investors is the potential tax savings. This month, Idaho Commerce announced that the U.S. Treasury approved 25 zones, including areas in Boise, Coeur d’Alene and Post Falls. The new Opportunity Zone designations take effect Jan. 1. An Opportunity Zone is a designated area where the federal government offers tax benefits to encourage private investment. The idea is straightforward: give investors a financial reason to put money into communities that could benefit from more economic activity. In Boise, the five areas identified by the city are Downtown, Shoreline, University District, South Boise Village and West Boise . These are general descriptions of the selected areas. The actual boundaries determine whether a particular property is included. In North Idaho, the officially designated list includes parts of Coeur d’Alene and Post Falls, as well as areas around Blanchard and Kellogg, Smelterville and Wardner. Other designated communities include Caldwell, Garden City, Nampa, Pocatello and Twin Falls. The state’s announcement provides the complete list and a link to look up the boundaries . The program connects investors with projects that need money. An investor who sells stock, real estate or a business at a profit may face a tax bill on that gain. By investing an eligible gain through a special investment vehicle called a Qualified Opportunity Fund, the investor may receive tax benefits. The fund puts that money into qualifying property or businesses within a zone. The IRS explains the basic structure here . Imagine a business owner who sells a company and wants to invest some of the profit. Across town, a developer wants to turn an underused property into apartments with shops on the ground floor. If the project is in an Opportunity Zone and meets the program’s requirements, an Opportunity Fund could connect that investor’s money with the development. The investor receives an ownership interest, and the project receives money to help move forward. Under the new rules beginning in 2027, a qualifying investor generally can delay tax on the invested gain for five years and reduce the amount of that gain subject to tax. Holding the investment for at least 10 years may also allow the investor to avoid federal tax on qualifying growth in the investment’s value. Coeur d’Alene also offers a potential partnership story. Idaho Capital Sun reported that Kootenai County and the Coeur d’Alene Tribe both sought designation for the local tract. The application summary identified vacant tribal land as an opportunity for investment involving the Tribe, local governments, and private developers. That possibility deserves attention, although the designation itself does not establish a finalized development partnership. For investors, those benefits can make a long-term investment more attractive. For developers and business owners, the program can help attract money from people willing to wait for a project to mature. That could support a new apartment building, the redevelopment of an older commercial property, or the expansion of a qualifying business. Residents may benefit from additional homes, employment, and services. Those outcomes are possibilities, not promises. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

items.body: Work continues on the new QTS data center in Eagle Mountain, Utah, on April 17, 2026. Today’s data center buildout has become the largest industrial boom since the railroad era of the 19th century, with $10 trillion in investment and almost twice the economic impact. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) The sheer size of investment in data centers is drawing concern as it surpasses all other historical booms and crowds out other more job-creating ventures. Until now, no industry had driven the U.S. economy with such force since the railroad expansion of the late 1800s, when titans battled one another to lay the transcontinental tracks that would connect America from coast to coast. Railroads in the 19 th century consumed about $173 billion in today’s dollars and created more than 2% of the nation’s annual economic output (GDP) over 20 years. Today’s data center buildout will dwarf that amount, with $10 trillion in investment, and now have almost twice the economic impact — nearly 4% of GDP. That’s according to a report created by a Columbia Business School professor, Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. States are starting to feel left out of the windfall, many having granted tax exemptions before the boom. Years ago, before artificial intelligence prompted a tsunami of building, states typically welcomed data centers supporting internet traffic, offering tax abatements and other perks. Many officials now are rethinking that approach as tax revenues take a bigger hit and high energy demands take a toll on affordability. Nevada , for instance, trimmed tax abatements and will ask data centers to agree to foot the bill for energy and water demands, in a September executive order from Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. States where data center costs will be concentrated over the three years are Texas ($638 billion), Virginia ($249 billion), Ohio ($169 billion) and Georgia ($160 billion), according to projections from Industrial Info Resources, a market intelligence firm. Southern states dominate the landscape for the number of data centers planned, with large numbers also proposed in Arizona, California, Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Indiana, North Carolina, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Washington state, according to a Pew Research Center report in April. The profitability of AI has yet to catch up with the expense of the buildout. “It is not a pretty picture right now,” said IIR’s senior vice president of research, David Pickering. “I think it will become profitable once things settle down a bit and more legislation is put in place to regulate how we handle AI. “The big players will no doubt find a way to make it profitable,” he said. There are signs the staggering cost of data centers is crowding out other investments such as housing. Over the past two years new construction value for data centers has more than doubled to $85 billion annually, while all other construction value has dropped 8%, according to a Stateline analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data as of August. As new data center value grew by $48 billion since 2024, new houses and apartments dropped by $29 billion, according to the data. items.body: A volunteer helps a young person fill out a form on National Voter Registration Day in 2025. For some young voters, abortion remains a defining issue, but for many others it ranks behind more immediate economic concerns. (Photo courtesy of Alliance for Youth Action) Editor’s Note: This story is part of Gen Z at the Ballot Box, a collaboration between States Newsroom and The 19th . Boise State University senior Cade Syvock opposes abortion. As president of the school’s chapter of the conservative group Turning Point USA, the organization founded by the late activist Charlie Kirk, Syvock helped coordinate anti-abortion protests on campus. But he’s not spending much time this fall campaigning against an Idaho ballot initiative that would restore abortion access. Not for lack of interest — he calls the proposed law “very, very extreme” because it allows abortions after viability in certain emergency cases — but because of pressing economic issues he’d rather be working on. “It’s not like everybody’s going out and getting abortions 24/7, but everybody is trying to find a home,” Syvock said. In Idaho and Missouri, where voters will decide the future of abortion access on Nov. 3, campaigns are trying to reach a generation dealing with rising living costs and skepticism toward politics. For some young voters, abortion remains a defining issue. But for many others, it ranks behind more immediate economic concerns. Idaho’s initiative would restore abortion access. Missouri’s measure seeks to reinstate a near-total ban jettisoned by voters two years ago. People pushing for and against both measures are making their appeals to young voters, using social media and canvassing to increase turnout on Election Day, but they’re competing against other issues for Generation Z’s attention. “I’m not saying that the abortion stuff is any less important than housing, but I think in terms of what young people are focusing on right now, it’s definitely dropped a little bit,” Syvock said. Gen Z politicians who want to make a change grapple with parties that aren’t always ready for them In most elections, it’s difficult for campaigns to achieve high turnout among young voters, especially in between presidential election cycles. Less than half of the 40 million Gen Z Americans between ages 18 and 29 who were eligible to vote in 2024 cast a ballot, a study by the Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement at Tufts University found. This year, the number of eligible Gen Z-age voters is estimated at nearly 50 million. But there are some signs that turnout could be higher this year. Nonpartisan youth vote organization The Civics Center noted a significant increase in voter registration among 18-year-olds compared with the 2022 midterms, from 35% to 42%. And the Tufts survey points out that there are many signs Gen Z is active and engaged on political subjects, but that connecting issues to candidates and ballot questions is the challenge. The majority of Gen Z adults support abortion access, according to a September poll from The 19th and YouGov. But there’s a gender gap: Women were more likely than men to say abortion should be always or mostly legal, 69% to 51%. Almost half of men versus 31% of women say it should be mostly or always illegal. The number of Generation Z Missourians who got involved in the 2024 initiative petition is not available, but more than 110,000 Idahoans signed the petition to put abortion access on the state ballot. About 7% of those signatures came from people between the ages of 18 and 25, and twice as many of those signatures came from women than from men. But some organizing efforts are made more difficult by local politics as well as increasing costs for food, housing and transportation. The 19th/YouGov poll found that 21% of Gen Z adults were worried about their ability to pay for groceries and 34% were somewhat worried. The attorney general serves a four-year term and receives an annual salary of $146,730. In a Republican-controlled state, Hickman’s election bid faces tough odds. items.body: Teachers in Bonneville School District will soon be required to sign a form certifying that they are either a biological male or female. District leaders say the new requirement will ensure compliance with state law governing public school bathroom usage. Multi-occupancy school restrooms must be designated for either males or females and only members of those biological sexes are allowed to enter, as required under Senate Bill 1100 , passed in 2023. “As a public school district, we have a responsibility to comply with Idaho law, regardless of our individual perspectives about it,” Superintendent Scott Woolstenhulme wrote in a letter to employees on Thursday. Woolstenhulme asked the school board to establish a “consistent process for employee verification.” Trustees on Wednesday night approved a resolution directing the superintendent to create a form that district employees must sign certifying their biological sex, as defined in Idaho code : “Male” means an individual who has, had, will have, or but for developmental or genetic anomaly or historical accident, would have the reproductive system that at some point produces, transports, and utilizes sperm for fertilization. “Female” means an individual who has, had, or will have, or but for developmental or genetic anomaly or historical accident, would have the reproductive system that at some point produces, transports, and utilizes eggs for fertilization. Idaho law — as established through 2024’s House Bill 421 — also declares that in human beings there are only two sexes, male and female. It was sponsored by Rep. Julianne Young, R-Blackfoot, and Rep. Bruce Skaug, R-Nampa. “An individual’s sex can be observed or clinically verified at or before birth; Rare disorders of sexual development are not exceptions to the binary nature of sex; In no case is an individual’s sex determined by stipulation or self identification,” Idaho law states. items.body: (UPDATED, 4:12 p.m. Tuesday, with comments from Secretary of State Phil McGrane.) In other states, even conservative strongholds like Kansas , voters have upheld abortion rights. But the abortion debate is not in Kansas anymore. Now it’s in Idaho. And it’s open warfare. Supporters and opponents have raised $9.7 million — so far — in the campaign over Proposition 1, a voter initiative to rescind Idaho’s near-complete abortion ban. Proposition 1 is by far the biggest political battle in the state, and, sensing opportunity, everyone wants a piece of the action. “Both sides are working to mobilize people to vote on that issue,” said Jaclyn Kettler, a political science professor at Boise State University. Proposition 1, explained For a quick and useful overview of what Proposition 1 would do, here’s a summary from Idaho Capital Sun . That also makes Proposition 1 a wild card. The hottest item on the ballot could drive turnout in other Nov. 3 elections — such as the governor’s and the state superintendent’s races; legislative races in Idaho’s scattered swing districts; and the $307 million in school levy requests . The high-powered opposition But for now, let’s focus on Proposition 1 itself. The parochial and partisan opposition is impossible to ignore. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has contributed $1 million in opposition to Proposition 1 . The Catholic Diocese of Boise has contributed $300,000 . The Idaho Republican Party, meanwhile, has gone all-in against Proposition 1. State GOP chairwoman Dorothy Moon has made the initiative nearly a staple of the weekly op-ed she sends to news outlets; six of her last 10 op-eds mentioned Proposition 1 in whole or in part. Last week, the GOP rolled out a news release touting near unanimous opposition to Proposition 1, from statewide elected officials and Idaho’s congressional delegation. “If there is one issue that unites Republicans across the ideological spectrum, it is that of life,” Moon said. (The only name not on the list: Secretary of State Phil McGrane. Asked about it Tuesday, Moon deferred to McGrane. On Thursday afternoon, McGrane described himself as a pro-life Catholic and a pro-life Republican, but said, as the state’s elections official he is staying neutral on Proposition 1. “It’s important that everyone has confidence in the process,” McGrane told EdNews.) For many Republicans, the Proposition 1 fight is more than just a little personal. After all, the initiative challenges abortion restrictions passed by an overwhelmingly Republican Legislature — and signed into law by Gov. Brad Little, who is seeking a third term next month. Little last week voiced his opposition to Proposition 1, saying it would “make abortion far more accessible in Idaho.” For the state’s prevailing party — and for two of the state’s largest religious groups — fighting Proposition 1 is a matter of seeking to protect the status quo. That alone is a driver, possibly the main one. The down-ticket implications: two recent examples The Republicans’ campaign against Proposition 1 is a marked departure from 2018. And it echoes 2024. Olivia Luna, a 21-year-old Idaho college student and Babe Vote leader, said a pair of 2023 state laws that removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification for voting hurt students and young people especially hard. House Bill 124 removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification for voting. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho State Department of Agriculture Director Chanel Tewalt told a committee of state legislators Tuesday that she believes Idaho’s population of invasive quagga mussels is very small and confined to limited sections of the Snake River. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE In September 2023, state officials used water sampling to c onfirm the presence of quagga mussel larvae for the first time in state history. During water sampling this year, state officials found eight veliger mussels, the larvae form of the mussels, Tewalt said during a meeting of the Idaho Legislature’s Natural Resources Committee at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. Scuba divers also found what Tewalt described as “a number of adult mussels” while searching the Snake River. The mussels, which were discovered in the Snake River near Twin Falls, can reproduce extremely rapidly, clog pipes and cover boat hulls. If left unchecked, Tewalt said the spread of quagga mussels poses serious threats to the state’s drinking and irrigation water, recreation industry, state budget and economy. Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US In an effort to completely eradicate all of the invasive species, officials with the Idaho State Department of Agriculture have been administering lethal copper chemicals into the affected part of the Snake River each year since the mussels were first detected. Compared to previous years, the amount of mussels discovered in water sampling is lower and the affected section of the Snake River is smaller this year, Tewalt told legislators. “What it would signify is a very small population,” Tewalt said. After detecting the mussels again this summer, the ag department moved forward with another round of copper-based treatments – with scuba divers injecting the chemicals in harder to reach nooks, crannies and fissures in rock. Chanel Tewalt serves as the director of the Idaho Department of Agriculture. (Courtesy of Idaho State Department of Agriculture) “Copper in the water means that reproduction cycle (for the mussels) is halted,” Tewalt said. Along with mussels, the copper also kills fish and other aquatic life in the river. This year, Tewalt said there have been fewer fish killed and that state officials are not stocking the sections of the river being treated with copper with new fish. Although the mussels were first discovered in water samples in 2023, Tewalt told legislators the mussels have likely been in the Twin Falls pool of the Snake River for longer. Water sampling and monitoring for quagga mussels is an ongoing, years-long process. When water temperatures warm up again next year, state officials will resume water sampling to check for more quagga mussels, state officials said. YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. SUPPORT
