items.body: Boise State University athletics has the green light to go $18 million in the red. With some reluctance, the State Board of Education approved the deficit spending plan Wednesday afternoon. Most of the $18 million will go into “revenue sharing” — direct payments to student-athletes. And Boise State will use a variety of budget reserves to cover the $18 million. “I personally don’t even like the term … deficit in athletics,” Boise State President David Hahn told State Board members. “Boise State is not running a deficit. We are managing our reserves, we are managing our finances. I’m putting that capital where it needs to be for success of all of the missions.” The $18 million figure is not necessarily unexpected. In August, Boise State Athletic Director Jeramiah Dickey warned the State Board that the cost of revenue sharing — and expenses tied to a move from the Mountain West Conference to a reformed Pac-12 conference — would drive the program into the red. Wednesday’s meeting brought the budget picture into more focus. Boise State is now projecting a $16.9 million deficit for the current budget year, which ends June 30. In August, Dickey pegged this year’s deficit at $14 million to $18 million. The university will provide the athletic department $3 million for debt service. The athletic department hopes to clear $2 million from special events at Albertsons Stadium. The stadium hosted two nights of the Banana Ball baseball barnstorming tour on July 31 and Aug. 1, and country singer Luke Combs is scheduled to perform at Albertsons Stadium on June 12, at the tail end of the budget year. Revenue sharing will increase to about $14.1 million, up from about $10 million. Colleges and universities can spend up to $21.6 million in revenue sharing, and the Boise State payments tie into “overall competitiveness” with rival programs, Dickey told board members. One unknown is the revenue Boise State will collect from the new-look Pac-12, now in its inaugural season. In time, Boise State expects to reap increased revenues from its new conference. But for this year, the university is budgeting for flat conference revenues, unchanged from its final season in the Mountain West, said Stacy Pearson, Boise State’s interim CFO. If the deficit exceeds $18 million, Boise State athletics would have to come back to the State Board for additional spending authority. The State Board approved the deficit spending plan unanimously, but not without discussion. Board member Shawn Keough — a former state senator who co-chaired the Legislature’s budget-writing Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee — said she was “really uncomfortable” with the vote. “I really don’t want to be here in a couple months or another year. Something has to give.” Board President Kurt Liebich said the deficit spending gives Boise State the flexibility it needs during a time of turmoil in college sports. The Senate has passed a college sports overhaul bill , but it is on hold in the House. “(We’re) giving you all the runway you need to figure it out, and I think you guys deserve that runway because of the sustained success you’ve had for 30 years,” said Liebich, who sits on a gubernatorial working group that has been studying the future of Idaho college athletics. Board member David Turnbull described Wednesday’s vote in stark terms. “The option is to basically put a bullet in Bronco sports if we don’t give them this runway.” The State Board is meeting at Lewis-Clark State College through Thursday.

The 107-page lawsui t filed in Ada County Fourth Judicial District Court alleges that the company has harmed Idaho children and deceived adults in violation of the Idaho Consumer Protection Act . “We have watched technology giants experience tremendous growth and gains while putting consumers, especially children, at significant risk,” Labrador said in a press release. “The safety of Idaho’s children cannot be an afterthought to runaway profit or technological advancements. We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry — not just one company.” Attorneys general in Arkansas, Montana, Nebraska, West Virginia, Iowa, Kansas and Arizona filed similar lawsuits in their state courts Wednesday, Reuters reported. Labrador, deputy attorneys general Matthew Maurer and Stephanie Guyon, and private attorneys from the Los Angeles and New York City offices of Kibler Fowler & Cave LLP brought Idaho’s lawsuit. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) A panel of Idaho lawmakers that studied issues in the health insurance market on Wednesday formalized plans to develop legislation to address a range of issues that affect access to health care. The Idaho Health Insurers Working Group voted to tee up plans to reform prior auth
items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on March 16, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) A panel of Idaho lawmakers that studied issues in the health insurance market on Wednesday formalized plans to develop legislation to address a range of issues that affect access to health care. The Idaho Health Insurers Working Group voted to tee up plans to reform prior authorization, a cost-control measure that health insurers use to deny covering certain treatments, and to target several other issues that the interim legislative committee heard about in its meetings in the last few months and through surveys it sent to insurers and health care providers. In a series of votes, the interim committee teed up a series of bills focused on health insurance that could be considered by the Legislature when it returns next January. Some of the other bills that could be drafted could address: Reducing delayed payments to providers, by setting standards for providers and insurers; Establishing uniform standards to credential health care providers through insurers; and Requiring the Idaho Department of Insurance, which regulates health insurers, to collect and present to the Legislature data about the timeliness of payments, and healthcare denial rates. That might also include information on one arbitration tool created by Congress that the state’s largest insurer, Blue Cross of Idaho, claims that a North Idaho microhospital heavily relies upon. Blue Cross argues the practice could drive up the cost of healthcare , and Congress is considering overhauling the tool. The potential prior authorization reform bill wouldn’t be the Legislature’s first attempt to address the issue, which some patients say can delay access to healthcare through drawn out timelines to issue decisions. Earlier this year, a bill, House Bill 611 , set out to require more transparency and establish timelines in the process, but it never received a committee hearing. Rep. Dustin Manwaring, R-Pocatello, listens to proceedings during the Jan. 12, 2026, Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee meeting at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Prior authorization also impacts healthcare providers. Providers in Idaho reported spending more time on administrative work to respond to prior authorization requests in recent years, according to data that committee co-chairman Rep. Dustin Manwaring, R-Pocatello, summarized. In 2025, an American Medical Association survey found that 92% of physicians reported negative patient impacts caused by prior authorization processes. The committee was formed after a now-resolved contract fallout between a hospital in East Idaho, Portneuf Medical Center, and the insurer that runs the health plan for state employees, Regence BlueShield of Idaho. In the coming years, the state plans to transition Medicaid, a health insurance public assistance program for people who have disabilities or earn low-incomes, from being state-run to being managed by private health insurance companies . (Photo illustration by Getty Images) The political action committee opposing Idaho’s Proposition 1 abortion rights initiative collected nearly $1.5 million since the end of September, buoyed by two large donations from churches. The Too Extreme for Idaho PAC, reported the previously announced $1 million donation from the Salt Lake City-based Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints on Oct. 8. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise donated another $300,000 to the PAC opposing the initiative the next day. Supporters and opponents of Idaho’s abortion rights initiative, Prop 1, have raised millions Since Sept. 29, Too Extreme for Idaho received $153,985 from 32 individual people and $1.3 million from four organizations, including the two churches. Too Extreme for Idaho has raised a total of just over $4 million, campaign finance data shows. As of Monday, the PAC supporting the initiative, Idahoans United for Women and Families, brought in more than $630,000 since Sept. 29. The largest donation came from the federal Government that Works PAC, based out of Washington, D.C, which gave $250,000. Oklahoma-based billionaire philanthropist Lynn Schusterman donated $200,000 on Sept. 30, campaign finance data shows. Since Sept. 29, the PAC received $265,290 from 81 individuals and $370,000 from three organizations. In total, Idahoans United has collected more than $5.6 million. Independent expenditures for and against Prop 1 total more than $2.5 million Groups and individuals spent more than $2.5 million combined to support and oppose Prop 1 in independent expenditures, which includes spending by organizations or individuals spent directly to support or oppose a ballot measure. The Idaho Secretary of State’s office in late September and early October began sharing a message with those filing campaign finance reports to request that any spending for or against a ballot initiative, constitutional amendment or advisory question be reported as an independent expenditure to help “voters more easily find and understand spending related to ballot measures.” The notice, first uploaded to the campaign finance reporting portal the last week of September and then updated on Oct. 7, also asked filers to amend previous campaign finance reports to classify spending related to ballot measures as independent expenditures. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Lands) More than 80% of the wildfires that the Idaho Department of Lands has responded to this year have been caused by humans, Director Dustin Miller told an interim committee of Idaho legislators Tuesday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE “This staggering figure just underscores the importance of not only a robust fuels mitigation program … but also a solid prevention program,” Miller told the Idaho Legislature’s Natural Resources Interim Committee during a meeting at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. Through the end of September, a total of 10,000 acres of land that the Idaho Department of Lands is responsible for protecting has burned. (That figure does not include the larger number of acres of federal land, such as U.S. Forest Service land, that burned in wildfires this summer.) Dustin Miller is the director of the Idaho Department of Lands. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Lands) The increase in human-caused fires is not new. In 2023, Miller also told a commission of statewide elected officials that he was investigating a spike in human-caused fires , the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Miller told state legislators the costs of wildfires are high, and several legislators immediately pushed for more answers. Through the end of September, the state’s wildfire costs were a little over $47 million, of which an estimated $19.8 million could be reimbursable from other agencies the state partners with, Miller said. In addition to the financial cost to taxpayers, fires also can also threaten the safety of firefighters and the public, destroy property and burn state endowment timber lands that generate funding for public schools and other beneficiaries. There is also the cost of rehabilitation and recovery following fire and the long-term effects caused by fire. Idaho legislators ask how state can recoup costs for human-caused fires While human-caused fires aren’t new, the 80% figure grabbed the attention of several legislators. Senate Majority Leader Lori Den Hartog, R-Meridian, asked Miller if the state was doing enough to go after the people who were responsible. Natural Resources Interim Committee Co-Chair Britt Raybould, R-Rexburg, asked if stronger penalties would be a deterrent. “Just something that encourages people to think a little more responsibly about how their behavior can have, not only the financial, but the environmental and property damage and all of the surrounding consequences,” Raybould said. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Miller told the committee that the state investigates the cause of every fire and attempts to recoup funding from individuals or groups that are deemed “negligent.” Sometimes the recovery process works well, Miller said, but sometimes it can take years to recover the money, and the state doesn’t always succeed. “Oftentimes we settle for less than what the suppression costs were,” Miller said. “We really try to work with the individual and their insurance companies,” Miller added. “These are taxpayers always, and we want to recoup as much as we can back to the general taxpayer. The Idaho Capital Sun spoke to Secretary of State Phil McGrane and his staff about some of the top concerns that have arisen this election season. Here are some of the most frequently asked questions: If I don’t fill in a response to every question, does my ballot still count? Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane attends the State of the State Address at the State Capitol building in Boise on Jan. 8, 2024. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) Voters can skip any question or race on their ballot if they choose to. McGrane had heard concerns from voters worried that if they didn’t fill out a response to one of the ballot questions, that the rest of their ballot would be thrown out. This won’t happen, he said. “Voters are not required to vote in every race on their ballot for it to count,” the secretary of state’s office spokesperson Joe Parris said in an email. “If they skip a question or contest, the remaining selections on their ballot will still be counted.” Can I write in a candidate or write in an answer to the state gun advisory question? Prospective write-in candidates in Idaho must file a “Declaration of Intent” to run with the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office, and the deadline to do so was Sept. 4. Voters may still write in a name, but that vote won’t count if it doesn’t go toward a registered write-in candidate. This year, the only write-in candidate who filed this declaration is independent gubernatorial candidate Jacob Burnett, according to the Secretary of State’s Office. For House Joint Resolution 4 , House Joint Resolution 6 , and Proposition 1 , there are only “yes” or “no” options to fill out on the ballot. The advisory question about selecting an official state gun has six choices of gun and no option to write in a response. Are signatures on absentee ballots verified, and how? Signatures on all absentee ballots are verified, Idaho Secretary of State’s Office officials said. Election staff members compare signatures on the ballots with voter registration, signature history on previous ballots, and driver’s license records to confirm a match before ballots are counted, Parris said. “Make sure you sign your own absentee ballot,” Parris said. “A common mistake is a spouse putting their return ballot in the wrong return ballot envelope.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. The state controller is a constitutional officer that serves as Idaho’s chief fiscal officer and serves on the Idaho State Board of Land Commissioners, which is commonly referred to as the Land Board. The position is for a four-year term and comes with an annual salary of $128,690. Mohan is not an accountant or IT professional, but he said his 30-plus years of experience evaluating and auditing government policy and programs has prepared him to serve as controller. He said he is running because he believes in accountability and transparency and did not want to see Woolf run unopposed, like Woolf did in the 2014 and 2018 general elections. “Since I decided to run and I started talking to people, the very first questions I get asked are, ‘Do we have a controller? State law gives counties the option to provide early voting, and flexibility on when that voting option can start. Some counties, such as Twin Falls and Bannock, start early voting Tuesday. items.body: The Boise Temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints as seen on Feb. 5, 2025. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has donated $1 million to an Idaho political action committee, or PAC, opposing the abortion rights initiative on the ballot this November. The donation went to the Too Extreme for Idaho Political Action Committee, which opposes the initiative. “While The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints remains neutral toward political candidates, it actively addresses ballot initiatives it believes carry significant moral consequences,” the church said in a statement. “Accordingly, the Church has joined a coalition of like-minded organizations and individuals in Idaho to dedicate resources toward defeating Proposition 1.” Supporters and opponents of Idaho’s abortion rights initiative, Prop 1, have raised millions If passed, the voter initiative would repeal Idaho’s abortion laws, enumerate rights related to reproductive health, and create liability protections for healthcare providers who provide abortion and other reproductive healthcare. The Idaho Falls radio station NewsTalk 107.9 first reported the donation on Thursday. The Idaho Capital Sun confirmed the donation with a spokesperson for the church on Friday. The large donation comes after Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador published an opinion in August that says churches are allowed to donate money to political campaigns — including for and against Proposition 1 — without disclosing their donors, as long as they don’t ask members to donate specifically for the campaign, Boise State Public Radio reported. Leaders from the church, widely known as the Mormon church, issued a letter against Prop 1 in September, the Salt Lake Tribune reported. The letter was read to congregations last month, the church’s assistant communications director Brian Whitlock said in an email. “Our long-held stance on abortion remains clear and unchanged,” the four-member U.S. Central Area Presidency of the LDS Church wrote in the letter. The church, which opposes elective abortions, posted its stance on abortion online . It allows for possible exemptions in cases of rape and incest, or in cases where a “competent physician determines that the life or health of the mother is in serious jeopardy,” or a “competent physician determines that the fetus has severe defects that will not allow the baby to survive beyond birth.” “Even these exceptions do not automatically justify abortion,” the statement said. “Abortion is a most serious matter. It should be considered only after the persons responsible have received confirmation through prayer.” Idaho’s abortion ban allows the procedure to prevent the death of the mother and in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors who provide abortions outside of those exemptions face felony penalties, including minimum prison time, and potential civil lawsuits brought by family members of the aborted fetus. Groups attached to Catholic organizations have contributed $7,161 to the Too Extreme for Idaho PAC, campaign finance reporting shows. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise contributed $2,000, and Catholic fraternal groups, called Knights of Columbus Councils, contributed the rest, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. items.body: President Donald Trump signed an executive order to allow dyed diesel on highways and prohibit the Internal Revenue Service from imposing the typical penalties for doing so. Some state restrictions remain on the fuel, but on Friday, Idaho Gov. Brad Little relaxed the Gem State's inspections of the fuel during harvest. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor) Idaho Gov. Brad Little signed an executive order Friday to suspend for 30 days state inspections of dyed diesel fuel in an attempt to lower costs for farmers and ranchers, according to the governor’s office. With election pressure mounting, states move to suspend fuel taxes Dyed diesel is diesel fuel with red dye in it and is exempt from federal and state motor fuel taxes. The tax-exempt fuel is only meant for certain approved off-road uses, such as for farming equipment, construction equipment and home heating. The dye helps regulators enforce this requirement. Idaho’s average diesel price was around $6.41 per gallon as of Friday, according to AAA fuel prices. Prices for oil products have risen this year largely because of restrictions on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz amid the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran, which have disrupted global supply chains. Diesel supplies have been in particularly short supply, NPR reported, and Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries have also affected global supplies. On Monday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to allow dyed diesel on highways and prohibit the Internal Revenue Service from imposing the typical penalties for doing so. Some state restrictions remain on the fuel. President Donald Trump hands off a newly signed executive order waiving federal taxes on red-dyed diesel to aide Natalie Harp during a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner) Little’s order signed Friday directs Idaho State Police and the Idaho Transportation Department to suspend inspection for dyed diesel while the agencies review Idaho’s policies and procedures, his office announced in a press release. The review will consider other state’s approach to dyed diesel enforcement and the agencies will make recommendations to Little for “efficient, effective, and practical inspection,” the release said. Little said in the press release that the timing of the order is meant to ease costs during harvest season. “Idaho farmers and ranchers work hard to feed our families, our country, and the world,” Little said in the release. “President Trump has made cutting red tape a priority, and Idaho is doing the same. We will continue looking for ways to give our farmers, ranchers, and working men and women on the road more freedom to do what they do best.” Legislative leaders in written statements said they supported the governor’s decision. “Idaho farmers and ranchers are facing high costs across the board, and expensive diesel is adding to the pressure during harvest,” Senate President Pro Tempore Kelly Anthon, R-Declo, said in the release. “This order provides some immediate relief while giving the state time to review these requirements and find a practical approach that supports our producers without adding unnecessary costs or red tape.” House Speaker Mike Moyle , R-Star, said suspending the inspections while the state reviews its policies “is a practical approach that puts common sense first and gives Idaho producers one less thing to worry about during harvest.” YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho state revenues beat their forecast for the third straight month and are now more than $90 million ahead of projections to begin Fiscal Year 2027, Gov. Brad Little announced Friday. For September, general fund revenues exceeded their forecast by $39 million, or 7%, according to the September General Fund Revenue Report issued by the Idaho Division of Financial Management. Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s state government runs on a fiscal year calendar that begins July 1 each year. Through the first three months of Fiscal Year 2027, state revenues are now up by $90.3 million, or 6.8%. The surging revenues in this year’s state budget are a stark contrast to last year, when Little and Idaho state legislators approved near across-the-board budget cuts for almost all state agencies, programs and departments to pay for federal tax cuts President Donald Trump signed into law through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and to ensure the state passed a balanced budget, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. State revenues were also up in July and August. “Idaho’s strong revenue growth is encouraging and reflects the strength of our economy, but we must remain disciplined and make spending decisions based on what we can responsibly sustain,” Little said in a written statement Friday afternoon. “The difficult decisions we made last year put us in a stronger fiscal position, and we need to continue prioritizing the investments that matter most to Idahoans while protecting our long-term financial stability.” Income tax withholdings are driver of state revenue increase Individual income tax withholdings are a big part of the revenue increase. The September General Fund Revenue Report said individual income tax collections are up 18.3% fiscal year to date. “It appears that employees are getting lots of hours of work and that there may be some bonus activity being paid by employers,” Idaho Division of Financial Management officials wrote in the September revenue report. Idaho’s governor will begin the 2027 legislative session in January by presenting budget recommendations for next year to the Idaho Legislature. items.body: Ada County election workers sort hundreds of absentee ballots for the 2026 general election on Oct. 1, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) In 2007, Idaho lawmakers passed a law to make English the state’s official language. That law, which is still on the books , requires English to be used as “the sole language of government.” But it lists many exceptions to its requirement that government documents be in English, such as for law enforcement or for “public health and safety needs,” to ensure public schools can teach students who are learning English and to ensure colleges and so universities can “pursue educational purposes.” 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More In this year’s general election on Nov. 3, Idaho voters will decide on whether to amend the state’s constitution to declare English as the state’s official language. But what isn’t immediately clear, some say, is whether the amendment will end existing exemptions in state law that allow languages other than English to be used by government agencies. The proposed constitutional amendment’s only exception allows the government to use other languages when required by federal law, such as in schools and, in some cases, election administration. “It’s not entirely clear, honestly, how much it would change things,” said University of Idaho law professor Richard Seamon, who has taught at the school for 30 years. The proposed amendment, passed by the Idaho Legislature to be placed on the ballot through House Joint Resolution 6 in 2025 , calls for English to be used in “all public proceedings, public documents, public instruction, and any other public acts of any public institution of the state of Idaho.” Here’s what the amendment will look like on your ballot: .indent2Container { margin-left: 1em; border-left: solid 1px var(--brand_one); padding-left: 2em; } “Shall Article X of the Constitution of the State of Idaho be amended by the addition of a new Section 8, to provide that the English language shall be the official language for the state of Idaho, and to further provide that, except as required by federal law, English shall be used in all public proceedings, public documents, public instruction, and any other public acts of any public institution in the state of Idaho?” To pass, the amendment needs support from at least 50% of voters.
